item.title: Hackers Exploit Cisco Expressway Flaw CVE-2026-76466 to Breach Russian Organization (2026)
item.description:
Cisco Expressway flaw CVE-2026-76466 is being exploited to gain root access and move from exposed devices into internal networks.

Attackers have exploited a critical flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score of 9.8) in Cisco Expressway to breach a Russian organization, and they moved fast once a working exploit went public.

“A vulnerability in the database service feature of Cisco Expressway Series could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with network access to a Cisco Expressway device to execute arbitrary operating system commands as root.” reads the advisory.

An unauthenticated remote attacker can trigger the flaw to run commands as root on an affected device. Cisco shipped a fix on 21 October, so this wasn’t a zero-day by the time it got used.


The vulnerability is caused by persistent cookies and weak client certificate checks when TLS Verify Mode is enabled for clustering. An attacker with access to these cookies could connect to the database service and send specific RPC commands, potentially executing arbitrary commands with root privileges on the affected device.

Russian security firm F6 says this is the first known case of the flaw being exploited in the wild, and it happened on Expressway X15.5.3 devices after a proof-of-concept exploit appeared on GitHub. The attackers started with two internet-facing Expressway boxes.

“The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices.” reads the advisory by F6. “Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization’s internal network. After obtaining root access, the attackers began preparing tooling for further lateral movement across the infrastructure.”


The attackers used custom Python scripts to scan networks, find accessible SMB resources, connect to SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories. Their goal was to steal credentials and other sensitive information.

F6’s analysts think AI tools helped write those scripts, judging by the comments and fix descriptions left inside them, which is a strange kind of courtesy from an intruder.

F6 published indicators tied to the activity: two IP addresses, a telltale “[email protected]” entry in the Erlang system log on affected devices, and Python scripts staged under a specific disk path.

“One of the key indicators of successful exploitation is the appearance of a nodeup ‘[email protected]’ entry in the Erlang system log (erlang.log) on affected Cisco Expressway devices.” states F6. “Such an entry indicates that a connection was established with an Erlang node whose identifier corresponds to the known exploitation mechanism — CVE-2026-76466. When such events are detected, organizations should review other logs and artifacts to confirm whether compromise has occurred.”

Nobody has linked the attack to a known group yet, so treat this as an active technique without a named author. If you run Expressway, update now, hunt for those indicators, and don’t assume a clean edge device means a clean network behind it.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Cisco)

item.title: JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard Report Third-Party Data Breaches After N0n Claims
item.description:
JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard disclose third-party data breaches after the N0n extortion group claims to have stolen customer information.

The disclosures involving JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard highlight a familiar but often underestimated security problem: the risks introduced by third-party service providers. All three companies have confirmed incidents involving external vendors after the N0n extortion group claimed it had stolen customer information and published data allegedly taken from their systems.

The important distinction is that the companies haven’t reported breaches of their own payment infrastructure. Instead, the incidents appear to involve information held by outside providers, showing how a security failure at a supplier can expose data belonging to major financial institutions and their customers.

JPMorgan said the attackers may have accessed marketing information held by its service providers, including customer names and email addresses.

“Based on our ​investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names ‌and email addresses,” a JPMorgan spokesperson told Reuters, adding that the company would be contacting the affected customers directly.

The bank stressed that its services weren’t affected and that the incident had no connection to the technical problems some customers experienced earlier in the week. Where necessary, it plans to contact affected customers and offer free credit monitoring.

Visa confirmed that the incident it was investigating involved a third-party provider in the Asia-Pacific region. The company said its own systems hadn’t been affected and that there was no evidence that payment information, including card numbers, had been exposed.

Mastercard also acknowledged a security incident at an external provider. The company said the exposure involved a limited number of email addresses belonging to a small group of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefits program. It stressed that the information wasn’t related to payments and that its payment network remained fully operational.

The N0n group had listed the three companies on its leak site on November 16, claiming to have obtained customer engagement and marketing data. It subsequently published the allegedly stolen information and marked the companies as having refused to pay. The group’s claims should be distinguished from the information independently confirmed by the companies.

The scale of the alleged exposure is significant. According to Reuters’ review, the JPMorgan-related files contained more than 16,000 customer email addresses, some associated with phone numbers and postal codes. Researchers also identified what appeared to be 124 email addresses belonging to bank employees.

The Visa dataset reportedly contained thousands of customer email addresses, phone numbers and marketing campaign records, mainly relating to Asia-Pacific markets. The available information also suggests that the exposure wasn’t limited to customer contact details, although the authenticity and completeness of the files remain important considerations.

Neither JPMorgan, Visa nor Mastercard has identified the affected service providers or disclosed the total number of customers involved. This leaves important questions unanswered, including how attackers accessed the providers’ systems, how long they maintained access and what security controls failed.

Even when attackers don’t obtain card numbers or account credentials, names, email addresses and phone numbers can be valuable. Criminals can use this information to create convincing phishing messages, impersonate financial institutions and target customers with fraudulent calls or messages. A message that includes a person’s name and references a genuine banking relationship is much more likely to attract attention.

For this reason, third-party risk management needs to go beyond contractual security requirements and periodic questionnaires. Organizations should know what information suppliers can access, limit the data they share, review access privileges and require timely incident reporting. They should also verify that providers apply appropriate security controls and have effective procedures to detect and contain intrusions.

The N0n group emerged in September and has listed roughly 200 alleged victims on its leak site. Its claims against the three financial companies show how cyber extortion can affect organizations through their suppliers, even when their core infrastructure and services remain operational.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, newsletter)

item.title: CVE-2026-23871: WhatsApp Bug Helped Scammers Make Messages Look Legitimate (2026)
item.description:
WhatsApp patched three security flaws, including one exploited in a real scam campaign to make fraudulent messages appear more credible.

WhatsApp’s November security advisory fixes three flaws, including CVE-2026-23871, a vulnerability in Click to WhatsApp ads affecting WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business for Android versions earlier than 2.26.17.4.

“Incomplete validation of external ad-reply URLs in WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android before 2.26.17.4 could have caused a target’s device to reveal its IP information to an attacker if an attacker sent media from an attacker-controlled URL when a crafted Click to WhatsApp ad-reply message was rendered and displayed in a message thread.” reads the advisory. “This issue may have been abused in conjunction with specific spam messages.”

The issue was caused by incomplete checks on external ad-reply URLs. An attacker could use a server under their control to send media through a crafted ad-reply message. When the message appeared in a chat, it could cause the victim’s device to reveal its IP address to the attacker.

SecurityWeek reported that WhatsApp discovered the flaw while investigating a real scam campaign. The company’s security team found that a scammer was exploiting the issue to make fraudulent messages appear more credible.

“Our team found this issue while disrupting a scam campaign, and we believe a scammer was using it to make their scam message seem more credible.” a WhatsApp spokesperson told SecurityWeek.

The second fix is more serious on paper, though WhatsApp has seen no sign it was ever used. CVE-2026-102769 is a SQL injection on WhatsApp for Android before 2.26.35.74, triggered when someone taps a specially crafted “order details” message sent from an unofficial client.

“A SQL injection vulnerability when the recipient tapped on a specially crafted “order details” message from an unofficial client in WhatsApp for Android prior to version 2.26.35.74 could have allowed deletion of locally-stored WhatsApp files and, only if the user is online at time of receipt, leaked one bit of information asked by the attacker about the user’s chat database via an induced-crash delivery receipt timing sidechannel.” continues the report.

The company is not aware of attacks in the wild exploiting this flaw.

The third, CVE-2026-44908, lives deeper in WhatsApp’s infrastructure than in the app itself. It affects the remote-attestation verifier that confirms trust with Meta AI’s confidential computing backend, across WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business on iOS, Android and Mac. Someone positioned inside Meta’s own infrastructure could, in theory, have presented a certificate signed by the wrong key to bypass the hardware root of trust, but such a certificate would first need to appear on a public transparency ledger, and WhatsApp says that ledger shows every published certificate checks out clean.

These issues come after two fixes released in May. One addressed a bug in Instagram Reels message handling that could make another person’s device load media from an attacker-controlled URL. The other fixed a Windows attachment-spoofing trick. By adding a NUL byte to a filename, an attacker could make an executable file look like a normal document. Meta received reports of both flaws through its bug bounty program, and there is no evidence that attackers exploited them.

Of the three new flaws, only one was used in a real-world scam. It also had the lowest technical impact. This shows that scammers don’t always need to exploit serious vulnerabilities or gain access to a device. A convincing message can be enough to deceive a victim. Make sure you update WhatsApp on all your devices. The fixed versions vary across iOS, Android, Mac, Windows and WhatsApp Business.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, CVE-2026-23871)

item.title: U.S. CISA adds Cisco Expressway, SAP NetWeaver, Broadcom VMware vCenter, and Apache Roller flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
item.description:
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds Cisco Expressway, SAP NetWeaver, Broadcom VMware vCenter, and Apache Roller flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added Cisco Expressway, SAP NetWeaver, Broadcom VMware vCenter, and Apache Roller vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog:

  • CVE-2025-42884 SAP NetWeaver Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Data Query Logic Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-76466 Cisco Expressway Series Use of Hard-coded Credentials Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-123890 VMWare vCenter Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-129448 Apache Roller Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability

The first vulnerability added to the catalog is CVE-2025-42884 (CVSS score of 6.5), affecting SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal. The flaw allows an unauthenticated attacker to inject JNDI environment properties or provide a URL used during JNDI lookup operations. This could give the attacker access to an unintended JNDI provider and allow them to disclose or modify server information. CISA added the vulnerability to its KEV catalog on November 20, 2026, confirming that it has been exploited in the wild. However, no public reports have identified the attackers or provided details about the campaigns in which they used the flaw.

The second vulnerability is CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score of 9.8), a critical flaw affecting Cisco Expressway Series. The vulnerability involves hard-coded credentials and insufficient validation of client certificates in clustered deployments. An attacker who obtains persistent cookies can connect to the device’s database service and execute specific remote procedure calls, potentially running arbitrary operating system commands with root privileges. According to cybersecurity firm F6, attackers exploited the flaw to breach clustered Cisco Expressway devices at a Russian organization shortly after a public proof-of-concept exploit became available. They then prepared tools for lateral movement across the victim’s network and accessed sensitive information. The activity has not been attributed to a known threat actor.

The third vulnerability is CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score of 9.8), an authentication bypass affecting VMware vCenter. The flaw resides in the VMware Directory Service and allows an attacker with network access to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant linked its exploitation to ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group previously tracked as UNC5221. According to their investigation, the group exploited the vulnerability as a zero-day in early September 2026, before Broadcom disclosed and patched it. The attackers used a custom tool named BONESAW to obtain sensitive vCenter data, hijack the SAML Security Token Service and create an administrator account for persistent access. The campaign also involved the exploitation of a BeyondTrust Remote Support vulnerability, CVE-2026-102764.

The fourth vulnerability is CVE-2026-129448 (CVSS score of 9.8), a critical deserialization flaw affecting Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4. The issue affects the XML-RPC endpoint, which accepts and deserializes vendor extension types before authenticating requests. An unauthenticated remote attacker can exploit this behavior to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable server. The Apache Roller maintainers have confirmed that attackers are exploiting the vulnerability in the wild, and CISA has added it to the KEV catalog. However, neither the project maintainers nor public reports have identified the threat actors behind these attacks or provided details about their targets and objectives.

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA orders federal agencies to fix the vulnerabilities by November 23.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, CISA)

item.title: Cairn AI Framework Used in Autonomous Zero-Day Exploitation
item.description:
Amazon uncovered AI-powered attacks on universities, where autonomous agents found a zero-day and gained root access without human guidance.

Amazon’s threat intelligence team found a Chinese-nexus actor running Cairn, an open-source AI pentesting framework, with one instruction for the agents: obtain shell access. No human chose the next step after that. The agents planned, executed, and adjusted on their own, and along the way they found a real zero-day in an open-source medical imaging application.

The discovery happened because the operator left their own server exposed. On 10 September, Amazon spotted a publicly hosted Cairn instance running with no authentication, which meant anyone could see the project configurations, the prompts, and the AI’s output. The prompts were in Simplified Chinese, and script timestamps matched China Standard Time, over a roughly 48-hour campaign against university IP addresses in East Asia, outside mainland China.

“On September 10, 2026, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn, an open-source autonomous AI penetration-testing framework, running without authentication. Because the operator left the server publicly accessible, the operational history of the platform was visible to anyone on the internet, including project configurations, actor prompts, and AI output. The operator wrote prompts in Simplified Chinese, and the timestamps in executed scripts were configured to China Standard Time.” reads the report published by Amazon. “Analysis of the instance revealed a campaign targeting IP addresses associated with universities in East Asia outside mainland China over an approximately 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026.”

Not all targets were vulnerable. At one university, the agents found a Redis server that did not require a password. They spent about 16 hours trying 148 different actions to break in. These included using Redis replication to load code, bypassing its security protections, changing configuration files, damaging memory, and exploiting Log4Shell in a nearby service. When these attempts failed, they tried another approach. They exploited an SSRF vulnerability in a Qdrant server on the same network to explore internal systems. They then tried different passwords against PostgreSQL, SSH, and other services. None of these attempts succeeded, but the AI agents kept changing their tactics and trying new approaches.

In another attack, the agents targeted a university GPU server for more than six hours. They collected about 80 real usernames from university websites, faculty directories, research lab pages, archived websites, and academic papers. They then tried more than 30,000 username and password combinations against SSH and other systems, including a VPN server and the university portal. These attempts also failed to gain access.

The medical imaging target is where it worked. The agents mapped the application’s framework and API endpoints, found an upload parameter, tested it for path traversal, and had it: a working file-write vulnerability. From first mapping the API to writing arbitrary files took about 11 minutes.

“Against a target running an open-source medical imaging AI application, the outcome was different. The agents identified the application’s framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter.” continues the report. “They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server.”

A later session turned that access into something worse. The agents wrote a Python reverse shell to sitecustomize.py, a file Python loads automatically on startup, then triggered a training endpoint that spawned a new process and imported the payload. That gave them a root shell with no human picking each step. Amazon assesses with high confidence this was a genuine zero-day, since no fix, advisory, or prior mention existed anywhere for the affected project.

The human operator came back once the agents had proven the bug worked. They handed the agents a proxy tunnel into a second university’s network, where a server ran the same vulnerable software, and told them to use that foothold to reach other machines. Amazon infers the actor had already used the same zero-day to set up that tunnel, which means one AI-found bug became the key to a second network.

Amazon notified the project’s maintainers, who shipped a fix and a security advisory. The affected universities weren’t AWS customers, so Amazon routed the warning through a government partner instead of reaching them directly. Separately, researchers at Gambit Security documented a different, financially motivated actor using the same framework against online retailers, so this isn’t a one-off experiment confined to espionage.

The speed of these operations is the most important point. An AI agent that can find and exploit a zero-day in just a few minutes can move faster than most security teams can investigate a single alert. Even when the attacks failed, the agents kept working for 16 hours without breaks or time limits.

Amazon uses honeypots and network traffic analysis to automatically detect some of this activity at no extra cost. The wider lesson is that defenders need to focus on reliable threat detection and fast responses.

“To keep pace, organizations should prioritize high-confidence detections that trigger automated response, with humans overseeing outcomes rather than reviewing every individual action.” concludes the report.

item.content:encoded:
Amazon uncovered AI-powered attacks on universities, where autonomous agents found a zero-day and gained root access without human guidance.

Amazon’s threat intelligence team found a Chinese-nexus actor running Cairn, an open-source AI pentesting framework, with one instruction for the agents: obtain shell access. No human chose the next step after that. The agents planned, executed, and adjusted on their own, and along the way they found a real zero-day in an open-source medical imaging application.

The discovery happened because the operator left their own server exposed. On 10 September, Amazon spotted a publicly hosted Cairn instance running with no authentication, which meant anyone could see the project configurations, the prompts, and the AI’s output. The prompts were in Simplified Chinese, and script timestamps matched China Standard Time, over a roughly 48-hour campaign against university IP addresses in East Asia, outside mainland China.

“On September 10, 2026, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn, an open-source autonomous AI penetration-testing framework, running without authentication. Because the operator left the server publicly accessible, the operational history of the platform was visible to anyone on the internet, including project configurations, actor prompts, and AI output. The operator wrote prompts in Simplified Chinese, and the timestamps in executed scripts were configured to China Standard Time.” reads the report published by Amazon. “Analysis of the instance revealed a campaign targeting IP addresses associated with universities in East Asia outside mainland China over an approximately 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026.”

Not all targets were vulnerable. At one university, the agents found a Redis server that did not require a password. They spent about 16 hours trying 148 different actions to break in. These included using Redis replication to load code, bypassing its security protections, changing configuration files, damaging memory, and exploiting Log4Shell in a nearby service. When these attempts failed, they tried another approach. They exploited an SSRF vulnerability in a Qdrant server on the same network to explore internal systems. They then tried different passwords against PostgreSQL, SSH, and other services. None of these attempts succeeded, but the AI agents kept changing their tactics and trying new approaches.

In another attack, the agents targeted a university GPU server for more than six hours. They collected about 80 real usernames from university websites, faculty directories, research lab pages, archived websites, and academic papers. They then tried more than 30,000 username and password combinations against SSH and other systems, including a VPN server and the university portal. These attempts also failed to gain access.

The medical imaging target is where it worked. The agents mapped the application’s framework and API endpoints, found an upload parameter, tested it for path traversal, and had it: a working file-write vulnerability. From first mapping the API to writing arbitrary files took about 11 minutes.

“Against a target running an open-source medical imaging AI application, the outcome was different. The agents identified the application’s framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter.” continues the report. “They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server.”

A later session turned that access into something worse. The agents wrote a Python reverse shell to sitecustomize.py, a file Python loads automatically on startup, then triggered a training endpoint that spawned a new process and imported the payload. That gave them a root shell with no human picking each step. Amazon assesses with high confidence this was a genuine zero-day, since no fix, advisory, or prior mention existed anywhere for the affected project.

The human operator came back once the agents had proven the bug worked. They handed the agents a proxy tunnel into a second university’s network, where a server ran the same vulnerable software, and told them to use that foothold to reach other machines. Amazon infers the actor had already used the same zero-day to set up that tunnel, which means one AI-found bug became the key to a second network.

Amazon notified the project’s maintainers, who shipped a fix and a security advisory. The affected universities weren’t AWS customers, so Amazon routed the warning through a government partner instead of reaching them directly. Separately, researchers at Gambit Security documented a different, financially motivated actor using the same framework against online retailers, so this isn’t a one-off experiment confined to espionage.

The speed of these operations is the most important point. An AI agent that can find and exploit a zero-day in just a few minutes can move faster than most security teams can investigate a single alert. Even when the attacks failed, the agents kept working for 16 hours without breaks or time limits.

Amazon uses honeypots and network traffic analysis to automatically detect some of this activity at no extra cost. The wider lesson is that defenders need to focus on reliable threat detection and fast responses.

“To keep pace, organizations should prioritize high-confidence detections that trigger automated response, with humans overseeing outcomes rather than reviewing every individual action.” concludes the report.

item.title: Cyberattack on Austrian Foreign Ministry Exposes Diplomatic Staff Data
item.description:
Austrian Foreign Ministry Hacked, Staff Contact Details Accessed

Hackers accessed Austrian Foreign Ministry records containing staff contact details, including employees at diplomatic missions abroad.

Austrian Foreign Ministry confirmed a cyberattack against its website that exposed staff contact information, including details of employees working at diplomatic missions abroad. The security breach occurred between November 12 and 13, during a global Microsoft outage, and raises questions about the security of government websites and the risks associated with services managed by external providers.

According to the ministry, attackers gained unauthorized access to a website operated by an external service provider. The intrusion was detected on November 13, and authorities said they stopped it immediately.

“”Between November 12 and 13, the foreign ministry’s website, which is operated by an external service provider, was accessed in an unauthorized ​manner,” the ministry said in a statement, adding that it happened ​during a global Microsoft outage.” Reuters reports.

The ministry confirmed that the hack was detected on November 13 ⁠and government staff stopped it immediately.

An investigation by a team of cybersecurity experts found that the intruders had viewed records containing the names and professional contact details of ministry employees. The information covered both staff at the ministry’s headquarters in Vienna and personnel working at Austrian diplomatic missions abroad.

“An investigation by a team of experts ​found that during the unauthorized access, data records were viewed that listed ​the names and work contact details of employees at ministry headquarters as well as at diplomatic missions abroad,” the ministry added.

The Austrian authorities have not disclosed how many records were accessed, whether the attackers copied the information, or how they managed to enter the website. They have also not identified the vulnerability or attack technique used.

The ministry stressed that the incident did not affect citizens’ personal information. According to Austrian public broadcaster ORF, the authorities reported the incident to the Federal Office for Cyber Security and the Data Protection Authority, while also launching additional technical security checks.

“The Foreign Ministry emphasized that it was taking the incident “very seriously.” The integrity of the infrastructure was of the highest priority. The systems were subject to strict security regulations and continuous monitoring, it stated. The incident had also prompted additional technical security checks.” states ORF. “The Foreign Ministry has been repeatedly targeted by cyberattacks. At the beginning of 2020, there was a serious cyberattack that lasted until February. In April 2022, there were cyberattacks involving phishing emails.”

The timing of the incident is also noteworthy. The ministry said the intrusion coincided with a global Microsoft service outage, but it hasn’t established any connection between the two events. A major service disruption can complicate incident response and monitoring, but the available information doesn’t show that attackers exploited the outage to gain access.

Attribution remains another unanswered question. The ministry hasn’t named any suspected country or threat group, and there’s no evidence linking this particular intrusion to a state-sponsored operation.

However, the incident comes against a difficult diplomatic background. Austria has maintained military neutrality but has politically supported Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. In July 2026, Vienna publicly accused Moscow of being responsible for a cyberattack against the Foreign Ministry in late 2019 and early 2020, joining eight other EU member states in condemning Russian cyber operations.

“The ministry did not suggest who might be responsible.” states Reuters.

Russia has repeatedly rejected Western accusations of hacking. Diplomatic tensions have also increased following Vienna’s decision to expel four Russian diplomats in October, bringing the total number of Russian diplomats declared persona non grata by Austria since 2020 to 18. Moscow promised an appropriate response and subsequently expelled an Austrian trade delegate working at the country’s embassy in Russia.

“Russia has repeatedly denied Western hacking allegations.” Reuters concludes.

Beyond the political context, this incident offers an important security lesson. Government websites may not host classified information or directly manage critical services, but they can still expose information that attackers can use to target employees, build convincing phishing campaigns, identify diplomatic personnel or gather intelligence about government operations.

The involvement of an external service provider also deserves attention. Outsourcing website management doesn’t outsource security responsibility. Public institutions need visibility into their suppliers’ security controls, access privileges, logging and incident response procedures, and must ensure that these arrangements receive regular independent checks.

Names and professional email addresses might appear to be low-value information, but they can help attackers prepare highly targeted operations. In diplomatic environments, even basic contact details can provide useful intelligence for social engineering and further intrusions.

Protecting government infrastructure also means protecting the people whose information and professional relationships can become the starting point for the next cyberattack.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Austrian Foreign Ministry)

item.title: Signal Is Blocking AI Agents From Reading Your Screen
item.description:
Signal is blocking OS-level AI agents from reading its app on iOS 27 and Android, warning that Gemini and Siri AI threaten its privacy guarantees.

Signal is restricting new AI agents built into iOS 27 and Android from capturing its data, president Meredith Whittaker announced. The company already did something similar on Windows last year, blocking screenshots to stop Microsoft’s Recall from capturing Signal messages by default. Now it’s doing the same wherever it can detect an AI assistant trying to read the Signal screen.

The process is simple, but it raises serious privacy concerns. Operating system-level AI agents, such as Google’s Gemini Intelligence and Apple’s Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI, scan the content displayed on your screen so they can answer questions and perform tasks for you.

This means these AI agents can capture your Signal data and use it to answer your questions and carry out your requests.

“In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.” reads the announcement. “The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”

Signal’s security model is based on open-source code and encryption that has been formally checked and reviewed by independent researchers for more than a decade. However, this protection can’t help if an AI agent reads your messages directly from the screen before encryption becomes relevant. Once captured, the data may be stored in a local database or sent to a remote server used by the AI agent, completely outside Signal’s control.

Google, Apple, and Microsoft aren’t just three companies among many here.

“these three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem.” continues the report. “Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy.”

When the ocean starts working against the fish swimming in it, the fish can’t simply find a different ocean.

Signal’s fix is narrow: block screenshots on iOS 27, and block AI assistant screen capture attempts on Android. Users can turn the protection off in settings if they want to take screenshots, but doing so exposes their messages, and their contacts’ messages, to the same agents Signal is trying to keep out. The company is upfront that this doesn’t close every door, since an agent could still reach app data through the filesystem rather than the screen.

MacOS gets no protection at all right now, because Apple and Microsoft don’t give developers a clean way to block AI access without wrecking the normal user experience. Signal says it spent real engineering time just doing forensic work across Android and iOS to figure out what these AI systems actually do with app data, because the documentation isn’t there. That’s a strange place for a company Signal’s size to be: reverse-engineering the privacy behavior of the platforms it depends on.

Signal is asking Apple, Google, and Microsoft to take two specific steps. First, they should give app developers a clear way to prevent AI agents from accessing their data, including information on the screen, files, notifications, and APIs. Second, they should explain exactly how these AI agents access, collect, and process user data.

Signal also raises concerns about third-party AI agents such as Meta’s Muse, which can use accessibility permissions that users originally granted for other purposes. The company adds that confidential computing doesn’t solve the problem because the platform still controls the privacy decision, not the app developer or the user.

Signal says it’s already talking with Google and Apple about better support for apps that handle sensitive information. The company is cautiously optimistic, but whether these discussions lead to real changes will depend on what the two companies actually do over the coming year.

Signal frames the stakes plainly for anyone tempted to see this as one company’s problem.

“We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data.” the report cocludes. “Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.”

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Signal)

The company already did something similar on Windows last year, blocking screenshots to stop Microsoft’s Recall from capturing Signal messages by default. Now it’s doing the same wherever it can detect an AI assistant trying to read the Signal screen.

The process is simple, but it raises serious privacy concerns. Operating system-level AI agents, such as Google’s Gemini Intelligence and Apple’s Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI, scan the content displayed on your screen so they can answer questions and perform tasks for you.

This means these AI agents can capture your Signal data and use it to answer your questions and carry out your requests.

Signal’s security model is based on open-source code and encryption that has been formally checked and reviewed by independent researchers for more than a decade. However, this protection can’t help if an AI agent reads your messages directly from the screen before encryption becomes relevant.
